title: The KV cache
objectives: Code a KV cache for the tiny GPT and compute its size for a large model.

screens.title: Work done twice
screens.prose: Level 2's sampler runs the whole window through the model for every new character. Generating 32 characters, step 1 runs 1 position, step 2 runs 2, and so on up to 32.
screens.question: How many positions does it run in all?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Add the positions run at each step.

byKey.square: That is $32^2$. Step $k$ runs $k$ positions, not 32.
byKey.once: That is the number of new positions. Without a cache each step reruns the old ones too.

explain.text: 528 position passes for 32 characters: 496 of them repeat work already done. A cache keeps what does not change.

screens.title: What changes when a token arrives
screens.prose: In a causal model a position attends only to itself and earlier ones, so a later token never changes an earlier position's keys and values. Step through six tokens arriving.
screens.question: When the 6th token arrives, how many of the 5 cached key and value rows must be recomputed?

hints.text: Does an earlier position ever see a later token?

feedback.correct: None: the 5 rows stay as they were, and the new token adds one row.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Can a later token change an earlier position's keys?

byKey.all: They do not depend on the new token: the mask stops earlier positions from seeing it.
byKey.one: Only the new row is computed, and it was not cached before.

explain.text: Earlier keys and values never change, so we store them: the **KV cache**. Each new token computes one row and reads the rest.

screens.title: Why the cache is exact
screens.prose: With the cache, a new token computes its own query, key and value, appends the key and value, and attends over all cached rows.

widget.prelude:
import numpy as np

import gpt_ops_l2 as G

W = G.read_weights('gpt-w-embed.json', 'gpt-w-block0.json')
encode, decode = G.encode, G.decode


def ln(x, g, b):
    mu = x.mean(-1, keepdims=True)
    var = ((x - mu) ** 2).mean(-1, keepdims=True)
    return g * (x - mu) / np.sqrt(var + 1e-5) + b


def _logits_match(text):
    ids = encode(text)
    full = G.forward_logits(W, np.array(ids))
    c = new_cache()
    return max(float(np.abs(decode_step(W, c, t) - full[i]).max()) for i, t in enumerate(ids)) < 1e-10

mutants.source:
import numpy as np


def new_cache():
    return {"k": np.zeros((4, 0, 8)), "v": np.zeros((4, 0, 8)), "pos": 0}


def decode_step(W, cache, token):
    x = W["wte"][token] + W["wpe"][cache["pos"]]
    qkv = ln(x, W["h0.ln1_g"], W["h0.ln1_b"]) @ W["h0.qkv_w"] + W["h0.qkv_b"]
    q, k, v = (qkv[j * 32:(j + 1) * 32].reshape(4, 1, 8) for j in range(3))
    cache["k"] = np.concatenate([cache["k"], k], axis=1)
    cache["v"] = np.concatenate([cache["v"], v], axis=1)
    s = q @ cache["k"].transpose(0, 2, 1) / np.sqrt(8)
    a = np.exp(s - s.max(-1, keepdims=True))
    a = a / a.sum(-1, keepdims=True)
    x = x + (a @ cache["v"]).reshape(32) @ W["h0.proj_w"] + W["h0.proj_b"]
    h = np.maximum(ln(x, W["h0.ln2_g"], W["h0.ln2_b"]) @ W["h0.fc_w"] + W["h0.fc_b"], 0)
    x = x + h @ W["h0.out_w"] + W["h0.out_b"]
    cache["pos"] += 1
    return ln(x, W["lnf_g"], W["lnf_b"]) @ W["head_w"] + W["head_b"]


def generate_cached(W, prompt, n, seed):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    ids = encode(prompt)
    cache = new_cache()
    for t in ids[-32:]:
        z = decode_step(W, cache, t)
    for _ in range(n):
        p = np.exp(z - z.max())
        ids.append(int(rng.choice(65, p=p / p.sum())))
        z = decode_step(W, cache, ids[-1])
    return decode(ids)

import numpy as np


def new_cache():
    return {"k": np.zeros((4, 0, 8)), "v": np.zeros((4, 0, 8)), "pos": 0}


def decode_step(W, cache, token):
    x = W["wte"][token] + W["wpe"][cache["pos"]]
    qkv = ln(x, W["h0.ln1_g"], W["h0.ln1_b"]) @ W["h0.qkv_w"] + W["h0.qkv_b"]
    q, k, v = (qkv[j * 32:(j + 1) * 32].reshape(4, 1, 8) for j in range(3))
    cache["k"] = np.concatenate([cache["k"], k], axis=1)
    cache["v"] = np.concatenate([cache["v"], v], axis=1)
    s = q @ cache["k"].transpose(0, 2, 1) / np.sqrt(8)
    a = np.exp(s - s.max(-1, keepdims=True))
    a = a / a.sum(-1, keepdims=True)
    x = x + (a @ cache["v"]).reshape(32) @ W["h0.proj_w"] + W["h0.proj_b"]
    h = np.maximum(ln(x, W["h0.ln2_g"], W["h0.ln2_b"]) @ W["h0.fc_w"] + W["h0.fc_b"], 0)
    x = x + h @ W["h0.out_w"] + W["h0.out_b"]
    cache["pos"] += 1
    return ln(x, W["lnf_g"], W["lnf_b"]) @ W["head_w"] + W["head_b"]


def generate_cached(W, prompt, n, seed):
    return G.sample_text(W, prompt, n, seed=seed)

screens.title: Cache the queries too
screens.prose: A colleague adds the queries to the cache "to be safe": every step stores the new token's query beside its key and value.
screens.question: What does caching the queries buy?

options.text: Nothing: a query is used once, by its own position
A faster next step, since fewer arrays are recomputed
options.why: No later step uses an old query, so nothing is saved.

options.text: Exact logits, which the KV cache alone does not give
options.why: The KV cache is already exact.

options.text: It is needed, or attention cannot be computed
options.why: A new token needs only its own query, against the cached keys.

hints.text: Which arrays does a later token read?
Its own query meets the earlier keys and values.
An old query is never read again.

feedback.correct: Old queries are never read: caching them only spends memory.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Which arrays do later tokens read?

byKey.speed: That is the trap: nothing later reads an old query, so storing it saves no work and costs memory.

explain.text: The cache holds keys and values because later tokens read them; a query is used once and thrown away.

screens.title: Past the window
screens.prose: The tiny GPT learns one position embedding for each of 32 positions. Once 32 ids are in the window, the next character is predicted from the last 32 ids, each one place earlier than before.
screens.question: What happens to the cached keys and values when the window slides?

options.text: Computed at the old positions, they are stale: re-run the window
Drop the oldest row and keep the other 31 rows
options.why: Every kept row carries its old position embedding, one place out. The result no longer matches the model.

options.text: Keep every row and let the cache grow past 32
options.why: There is no embedding for position 32: the model has a hard limit of 32 positions.

options.text: Nothing: keys and values do not depend on position
options.why: They depend on the input, which includes the position embedding.

hints.text: Each row was computed with its position's embedding.
After the slide every id has a new position.

feedback.correct: With learned absolute positions every row goes stale when the window slides, so the tiny GPT re-runs the last 32 ids.
feedback.generic: Not quite. What does each cached row depend on?

byKey.drop: That keeps rows whose position embeddings are one place out, so the logits change. Models with relative positions can slide a cache; this one cannot.

explain.text: Past the window the tiny GPT gains nothing from the cache. Models whose positions are relative can keep a sliding cache; every model still has a limit past which the cache is cropped.

screens.title: GPT-2 small's cache
screens.prose: Each layer caches a key and a value of width $d$ for every position. GPT-2 small has 12 layers of width 768 and a context of 1,024; store the cache in bf16.
screens.question: How many MiB is the cache for one full sequence? (1 MiB is $2^{20}$ bytes.)

feedback.generic: Not quite. Multiply all five factors, then divide by $2^{20}$.

byKey.keys: That counts the keys only. Values are cached too.
byKey.mb: That is millions of bytes. A MiB is $2^{20}$.

explain.text: 36 MiB a sequence: small beside GPT-2's weights, but it is per sequence, and grows with the length.

screens.title: A 7B-like model's cache
screens.prose: A 7B-like model has 32 layers of width 4,096 and serves sequences of 4,096 tokens in bf16. One sequence's cache is $2 \times 32 \times 4{,}096 \times 4{,}096 \times 2$ bytes $= 2$ GiB.
screens.question: How many GiB is the cache for a batch of 16 sequences?

hints.text: Each sequence has its own cache.

feedback.correct: $16 \times 2 = 32$ GiB, more than the 14 GB of weights.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Each of the 16 sequences has a 2 GiB cache.

byKey.weights: That is the weights. The cache is separate, per sequence.

explain.text: 32 GiB of cache against 14 GB of weights: at long contexts and large batches the cache, not the model, fills the memory.

screens.title: The cache rule
screens.prose:
A model with $L$ layers of width $d$, serving $B$ sequences of $T$ tokens at $b$ bytes a number, holds
$$\text{KV cache} = 2 \times L \times d \times T \times b \times B \text{ bytes}.$$
Each new token reads the whole cache and all the weights.
screens.question: Double the context $T$. What happens to the cache?

options.text: It doubles
It quadruples
options.why: The cache holds $T$ rows; the $T^2$ is the attention scores, never stored.

options.text: It stays the same
options.why: Every position adds a key and a value.

options.text: It halves

feedback.correct: Linear in $T$: twice the context, twice the cache.
feedback.generic: Not quite. How many rows does the cache hold?

explain.text: The cache grows linearly with layers, width, length and batch; the attention it serves costs $O(T)$ per new token.

widget.solution:
def kv_cache_bytes(layers, d, T, bytes_per, batch):
    return 2 * layers * d * T * bytes_per * batch

screens.title: Decoding at a batch of 1
screens.prose: Each new token of the 7B-like model reads all 14 GB of weights and its whole cache. At 4,096 tokens the cache is 2 GiB, $2{,}147{,}483{,}648$ bytes. Take the chip that moves 3.3 TB/s.
screens.question: How many tokens a second can it generate at most? Give the nearest whole number.

hints.text: Time per token: bytes over bandwidth.

feedback.correct: $16{,}147{,}483{,}648 / 3.3 \times 10^{12} \approx 4.89$ ms a token: about 204 tokens a second.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the bytes read by the bandwidth, then invert.

byKey.weights: That reads the weights alone, 4.24 ms a token. The cache is read too.
byKey.ms: That is milliseconds per token. Invert it for tokens per second.

explain.text: At a batch of 1 the speed is bytes over bandwidth: 236 tokens a second for the weights alone, 204 with a 2 GiB cache. The arithmetic barely matters.

screens.title: A long research conversation
screens.prose: An analyst keeps one long conversation with the 7B-like model. At 32,768 tokens of context its cache is 16 GiB, $17{,}179{,}869{,}184$ bytes, read with the 14 GB of weights for every new token.
screens.question: How many times longer does each new token take at 32,768 tokens than at the start? Give 2 decimal places.

hints.text: Time is proportional to bytes read.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare the bytes read per token.

byKey.cache: That is the cache over the weights. Add the weights to the cache first.
byKey.same: The weights are the same, but the cache is read too.

explain.text: Each token takes about 2.23 times as long: late in a long conversation every answer reads a 16 GiB cache as well as the weights, so it costs more too. Starting a fresh conversation with a summary resets it.

ideas: A causal model never changes an earlier position's keys and values, so a cache of them is exact: each new token computes one row and reads the rest.
The cache holds $2LdTbB$ bytes: 36 MiB for GPT-2 small at 1,024 tokens in bf16, 2 GiB per sequence for a 7B-like model at 4,096.
At a batch of 1 each token reads all the weights and the whole cache, so bandwidth sets the speed: 14 GB at 3.3 TB/s is 4.24 ms, about 236 tokens a second.
